q: What is Figure A, used in metal roofing systems where seams are folded multiple times to create a highly secure, weather-tight joint, often used in high-performance roofs?
n: A double-lock standing seam is folded over twice (360°) so the seam is very tight. It is used on low slopes and high-performance roofs. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual; metal roofing manufacturer literature.

q: What is Figure B, used in standing seam metal roofing systems that use a raised covering to protect panel edges and enhance water shedding, commonly seen in traditional roofs?
n: A batten seam joins panels at a raised batten (wood or metal) capped by a metal cover, protecting the panel edges and shedding water. It is a traditional standing seam look. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual.

q: What is Figure C, used in metal roofing to connect panels with a vertical joint that is typical in historic buildings and provides a strong mechanical interlock?
n: A tee seam connects panels with a T-shaped vertical interlock, a traditional mechanical joint on historic metal roofs. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual; metal roofing manufacturer literature.

q: What is Figure D, used in modern metal roofing to increase structural strength and drainage performance, often specified for contemporary roof profiles?
n: A trapezoidal rib profile adds depth for stiffness, so sheets span farther between purlins and drain water quickly. It is common on modern long-span roofs. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature (BlueScope, Union Galvasteel).

q: What is Figure E, used in standing seam roofs that allows panels to connect without the need for tools or mechanical folding, making installation faster and simpler?
n: Snap-lock panels have male and female edges that click together without seaming tools, making installation faster. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature; SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual.

q: What is Figure A used for, which is designed around pipes or vents that penetrate the roof to prevent water infiltration, ensuring that the joints are sealed and water does not enter the structure?
n: Vent (pipe) flashing is a boot or collar sealed around a pipe or vent that passes through the roof, so water sheds around the penetration. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual (penetrations).

q: What is Figure B used for, which is designed to seal the area where a skylight meets the roof, effectively preventing leaks by directing water away from the skylight opening?
n: Skylight flashing surrounds the skylight curb and laps under and over the roofing, directing water around the opening. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual; skylight manufacturer installation guides.

q: What is Figure C used for, which is designed to create a watertight seal around chimneys where they meet the roof, preventing leaks and water damage around the chimney structure?
n: Chimney flashing (step and counter-flashing) seals the joint where a masonry chimney meets the roof slope. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual.

q: What is Figure D used for, which is installed in roof valleys where two roof slopes meet, directing water away from the joint to avoid pooling and leakage?
n: Valley flashing lines the valley where two slopes meet and carries the concentrated runoff down to the eave. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is Figure E used for, which is designed to prevent water leakage at the intersections of roof systems with box gutters, ensuring a watertight seal at the joints?
n: Gutter apron flashing laps from under the roofing into the box gutter, so runoff drops into the gutter rather than behind it. Source: SMACNA Architectural Sheet Metal Manual (gutters).

q: Which roofing is most economical over its life because it has the lowest risk of leaks?
n: Long-span sheets run in one piece from ridge to eave, so there are no end laps to leak and fewer fasteners. That lowers maintenance and gives the best value over the roof's life. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature (Union Galvasteel, BlueScope).

q: What is the thickest metal roofing sheet available locally?
n: Locally roll-formed long-span sheets are generally made up to about 0.70 mm base metal thickness, with 0.40–0.50 mm common for houses. Source: Philippine metal roofing manufacturer product data.

q: Which local company makes concrete roof tiles?
o: Bryan Isaiah Trading and Construction Inc.
n: Riviera Filipina Inc. is a Philippine maker of concrete roof tiles. Source: Riviera Filipina company website.

q: Which of these is an eco-friendly roofing material?
n: Clay tiles are made from natural clay, last for decades, need no coatings and can be crushed and recycled, so they are an eco-friendly roofing choice. Source: Philippine Green Building Code (2015), materials; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What is the traditional minimum roof pitch required for a tiled roof?
n: Lapped clay and concrete tiles need a pitch of about 15°–20° or more so wind-driven rain cannot back up under the laps. 15° is the traditional minimum quoted for tiles. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof slopes); roof tile manufacturer literature.

q: What is the most cost-effective & economic type of roofing?
n: Pre-painted long-span metal sheets give the lowest installed cost per square meter for most roofs: one-piece runs, quick installation and fewer laps and fasteners. Source: Philippine metal roofing manufacturer literature; Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate.

q: What is one advantage of long-span roofing?
n: Long-span sheets have no end laps, so water has fewer joints to seep through. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature.

q: What is a key advantage of long-span roofing?
n: The key advantage of long-span roofing is that each sheet runs ridge to eave in one piece, eliminating end lapping. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature.

q: What is the usual maximum length of a long-span roof sheet?
o: Custom lengths up to what can be transported
n: Long-span sheets are roll-formed on site or in the plant to the exact length ordered. The practical limit is what can be transported and handled. Source: Metal roofing manufacturer literature (Union Galvasteel, BlueScope).

q: What is commonly used for purlins under GI roofing?
n: Cold-formed light-gauge C-purlins are the standard support for metal roof sheets over steel or wood trusses. Source: AISI S100 (cold-formed steel design); Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Which roofing material below requires fewer purlins due to its rigidity and span capacity?
n: Corrugated (and long-span) metal sheets get their stiffness from the corrugated profile, so they span about 0.6–1.2 m or more between purlins. Clay and cement tiles need battens at roughly 0.30–0.35 m. Polycarbonate is flexible and moves with heat, so it needs closer supports. Corrugated roofing therefore needs the fewest purlins. Source: Max Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (Roofing – purlin spacing); manufacturers' span tables for G.I./long-span roofing and polycarbonate sheets.

q: In a wooden roof frame, what supports the purlins?
n: In wood roof framing, purlins are held on the top chord by small wood blocks called cleats, which stop them from rolling or sliding. Source: Philippine carpentry practice; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: What are the members laid across truss top chords to carry roof sheets?
n: Purlins span across the top chords of the trusses and carry the roof sheets. Rafters and joists belong to other framing systems. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof framing).

q: What is the maximum spacing of 2×4 wood purlins under typical residential roof sheets?
n: 2" × 4" wood purlins under corrugated or long-span sheets are typically spaced at about 0.60 m on center for residential roofs. Source: Fajardo, Simplified Construction Estimate (roofing); manufacturer span tables.

q: Which of the following is NOT required in a roof system?
n: Camber is a slight upward curve built into a beam or truss during fabrication, not a member of the roof system. Sag rods, truss rods and queen posts are actual members. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated; AISC Code of Standard Practice (camber).

q: Which fastener for aluminum roofing has a pin head and a long shank and is set from one side?
n: A blind (pop) rivet has a pin (mandrel) through a hollow rivet. It is set from one side by pulling the pin, which suits thin aluminum sheets. Source: Metal fastening manufacturer literature; Ching, Building Construction Illustrated.

q: Where trees surround the house, which roof component is least recommended?
n: Under trees, gutters fill with leaves and clog, overflow and rot the fascia, so they are the least recommended component there unless leaf guards are fitted. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof drainage).

q: What is the line where two roof slopes meet at an inside corner and collect rainwater?
n: A valley is the internal intersection where two roof slopes meet and collect water. A hip is the external, ridge-like intersection that sheds water. Source: Ching, Building Construction Illustrated (roof forms).

q: What is the minimum slope recommended for a roof in degrees?
n: For corrugated and long-span metal roofs in Philippine rainfall, about 15° is the usual recommended minimum slope so laps shed water quickly. Source: Philippine metal roofing manufacturer installation guides.

q: What is the current corporate name of Jacinto Steel's color-roofing business?
n: Jacinto Steel's color-roofing business was relaunched in 2010 as JacintoColor Steel, Inc., which makes pre-painted roofing sheets. Source: JacintoColor Steel company website.

q: Which company is a known manufacturer of color steel roofing in the Philippines?
n: Colorsteel Systems Corporation is a Philippine manufacturer of color steel roofing and wall cladding. Source: Colorsteel Systems Corporation company website.

q: What roofing product is manufactured by Puyat Steel Corporation?
n: Puyat Steel Corporation is a long-established Philippine maker of galvanized corrugated roofing sheets. Source: Puyat Steel company references; Philippine steel industry listings.

q: Which of the following is a local supplier of clay roof tiles?
n: Riviera Filipina Inc. supplies roof tiles in the Philippines. Mariwasa makes floor and wall tiles, and Apo and Unitec are cement and other building products. Source: Riviera Filipina company website.

q: Which roofing brand sells the "Durarib" and "Duracorr" lines?
n: Durarib and Duracorr are Union Galvasteel Corporation's rib-type and corrugated roofing lines. Source: Union Galvasteel company website.
